blocks.tk: Seljuklar oguzlardy. Onunjy asyrda oguzlaryň köp taýpasy Syrderýanyň boýunda ýaşaýardy. Olar goýun, at we düýe saklaýardylar we mallary bilen bir ýerden başga ýere göçýärdiler. Bu taýpalaryň biriniň başynda Seljuk atly bir beg durýardy. Ol adamlary bilen Jent şäheriniň töweregine göçüpdi. Seljuk döwletiniň ady şu begden gelýär. Şol döwrüň ýazyjylary oguzlara köplenç “türkmen” diýýärdiler.
blocks.en: The Seljuks were Oghuz Turks. In the 10th century many Oghuz tribes lived along the Syr Darya, keeping sheep, horses and camels and moving with their herds from one pasture to the next. At the head of one group stood a chief called Seljuk, who had settled with his people near the town of Jand, not far from the river's mouth. The dynasty, and the empire it built, take their name from him. Writers of the time often called these Oghuz Turkmen, and modern encyclopedias still speak of the Turkmen Seljuks.

blocks.tk: On birinji asyryň başynda Seljuk begiň agtyklary, Togrul beg bilen Çagry beg, adamlaryny günorta äkitdiler. Olar Amyderýadan geçip, Horasana geldiler. Şol wagt Horasan Gazna soltanlarynyň elindedi. Seljuklaryň mallaryna giň öri meýdanlary gerekdi, ýöne Gazna soltany olary Horasanda islemeýärdi. Birnäçe ýyl uruş dowam etdi, seljuklar birnäçe şäheri aldylar.
blocks.en: Early in the 11th century two of Seljuk's grandsons, the brothers Tughril and Chaghri, led their people south across the Amu Darya into Khorasan, which then belonged to the sultans of Ghazni, the Ghaznavids. The herders needed wide pastures for their flocks; the sultan wanted them out of his lands. For several years the two sides fought, and the Seljuks took a number of towns.

blocks.tk: 1040-njy ýylyň maý aýynda Merw bilen Saragtyň arasyndaky çölde, Dandanakan galasynyň ýanynda uly söweş boldy. Gazna goşuny birnäçe hepde çölde ýöräpdi. Ýollarda suw azdy, esgerler we atlar aç hem ýadawdy. Seljuk atlylary çalt hereket edýärdiler. Seljuklaryň goşunynda takmynan on alty müň atly bardy. Söweşde seljuklar ýeňdi. Taryhçylar Gazna goşunynyň sany barada ylalaşmaýarlar.
blocks.en: The decisive battle came on 23 May 1040, in the desert near the fortress of Dandanaqan, between Merv and Sarakhs. According to Encyclopaedia Iranica, some 16,000 Turkmen horsemen under Tughril and Chaghri defeated the heavily armed army of Sultan Mas'ud I, which famine and drought had already worn down. Accounts of the sultan's army differ: some histories give it 50,000 men and war elephants, while the historian C. E. Bosworth judged that, hungry and demoralized by the day of the battle, it was probably no larger than the Seljuk force.

blocks.tk: Bu ýeňişden soň tutuş Horasan seljuklaryň eline geçdi. Togrul beg soltan boldy. Şol wagt Bagdatda Abbasy halyfy ýaşaýardy. 1055-nji ýylda Togrul beg halyfyň çakylygy bilen Bagdat şäherine girdi. Soňky ýyllarda Seljuk döwleti örän uly döwlet boldy: ol Merkezi Aziýadan Kiçi Aziýa çenli ýetýärdi.
blocks.en: The victory gave the Seljuks the whole of Khorasan and ended Ghaznavid rule there. Tughril took the title of sultan, and in 1055, at the request of the Abbasid caliph, he entered Baghdad, the caliph's seat. Under his successors the Great Seljuk empire stretched from Central Asia to Asia Minor.

blocks.tk: On ikinji asyrda Merw Seljuk döwletiniň paýtagtydy. Soltan Sanjar 1097-nji ýyldan Horasanyň hökümdarydy, 1118-nji ýylda ol tutuş döwletiň baş soltany boldy. Onuň tagty Merwdedi. Şol wagt Merw dünýäniň iň uly şäherleriniň biridi. Bir taryhçynyň pikirine görä, 1150-nji ýyla golaý Merwde iki ýüz müň töweregi adam ýaşapdyr. Bu ýerde alymlar, şahyrlar we ussalar ýaşaýardy, kitaphanalar köpdi.
blocks.en: Merv reached its height in the 12th century, as a capital of the Seljuks. Sultan Sanjar governed Khorasan from 1097, and from 1118 he was the senior ruler of the whole dynasty, holding court at Merv. In his time Merv was one of the largest cities in the world: the historian Tertius Chandler estimated that around 1150 it had some 200,000 people. It was home to scholars, poets and craftsmen, and rich in libraries.

blocks.tk: Ýöne Sanjaryň soňky ýyllary kyn geçdi. 1141-nji ýylda Samarkant şäheriniň ýanynda ol uly söweşde ýeňiş gazanyp bilmedi. 1153-nji ýylda oguz taýpalary Sanjara garşy çykdylar we ony ýesir aldylar. Soltan üç ýyl ýesirlikde ýaşady. 1156-njy ýylda ol gaçdy, ýöne bir ýyldan soň, 1157-nji ýylda, Merwde aradan çykdy. Sanjaryň ölüminden soň Seljuk döwleti bölünip gitdi. Onuň kümmeti häzir hem Gadymy Merwde dur.
blocks.en: Sanjar's last years were hard. In 1141 he suffered a heavy defeat near Samarkand. In 1153 Oghuz tribes, the very people his dynasty had come from, rose against him and took him prisoner. He spent three years in captivity, escaped in 1156, and died at Merv the following year, in 1157; with his death, Great Seljuk rule in Khorasan came to an end. His mausoleum, which you met in the A2 interlude on Ancient Merv, still stands there today.

blocks.title: Reading the Turkmen
blocks.text: Notice the pasts: *ýaşaýardy* and *göçýärdiler* describe how the Oghuz lived, *göçüpdi* looks back to an earlier move, *ýöräpdi* to the march before the battle, and the events of the story are in `-dY`: *boldy*, *ýeňdi*, *girdi*.

questions.q: When was the battle of Dandanaqan?
questions.explain: 1055 is when Tughril entered Baghdad, and 1157 when Sanjar died at Merv.

questions.q: Where did Sultan Sanjar hold court?
questions.explain: *Onuň tagty Merwdedi*: his throne was in Merv.

questions.q: On what do accounts of the battle disagree?
options: the size of the sultan's army
questions.explain: Some histories give 50,000 men; Bosworth thought the army much smaller by the day of the battle. *Taryhçylar Gazna goşunynyň sany barada ylalaşmaýarlar.*

sources.title: Dandānqān
sources.note: 8 Ramażān 431 / 23 May 1040, in the desert outside Dandānqān, between Marv and Sarakhs; some 16,000 Turkmen under Ṭoḡrel Beg and Čaḡrī Beg defeated the heavily armed army of Masʿūd I, weakened by famine and drought; Khorasan opened to the Saljuqs

sources.title: Battle of Dandānqān
sources.note: The decisive clash of 1040 between Masʿūd I (reigned 1031–41) and the nomad Turkmen Seljuqs; a fortress in the desert between Merv and Sarakhs; the Seljuqs attacked with 16,000 horsemen

sources.title: Battle of Dandanaqan
sources.note: The figure of 50,000 Ghaznavid soldiers in some accounts, and Bosworth's view (The Ghaznavids, 1963) that the starving, demoralized army was much smaller; the hit-and-run raids on the march to Sarakhs

sources.title: The Seljuqs and the Khwarazm Shahs
sources.publisher: UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, vol. IV (A. Sevim and C. E. Bosworth)
sources.note: Seljuq and his followers moved up the Syr Darya to Jand in the 10th century; Tughril and Chaghri brought up by their grandfather

sources.title: Sanjar
sources.note: Seljuq prince of Khorasan, governor appointed by Berk-yaruq, head of the dynasty after 1118; defeated near Samarkand in 1141; died 8 May 1157

sources.title: State Historical and Cultural Park “Ancient Merv”
sources.note: Merv as a capital of the Great Seljuk empire in the 11th–12th centuries; the mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar

sources.title: Ahmad Sanjar
sources.note: Ruler of Khorasan from 1097, sultan from 1118; captured by Oghuz tribes in 1153 and held until 1156; died at Merv in 1157

sources.title: Seljuk Empire
sources.note: Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 under a commission from the Abbasid caliph; the empire fractured after Sanjar's death

sources.title: Merv
